abstract: The reproductive success of flowering plants relies greatly on precise timing of the floral transition, which is finely modulated by a complex network of floral regulators. As a main floral integrator, FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) is also an essential constituent of the florigen that is transported from leaves to shoot apices to induce flowering. FT is specifically transcribed in leaf vascular tissues, where its production is suppressed by many flowering repressors, including the MYB transcription factor EARLY FLOWERING MYB PROTEIN (EFM). Here, we show that a plant CTD phosphatase, C-TERMINAL DOMAIN PHOSPHATASE-LIKE 2 (CPL2), suppresses FT expression in leaf vascular tissues by modulating the binding activity of EFM. CPL2 interacts with and dephosphorylates EFM to facilitate the binding of dephosphorylated EFM to FT chromatin, thereby inhibiting flowering. Our results suggest that CPL2-mediated dephosphorylation of the floral repressor EFM serves as a molecular switch, adding another layer of regulation to fine-tune FT transcription and ensure that flowering occurs at an appropriate time.

body:
Introduction
The reproductive success of flowering plants depends, to a large extent, on proper timing of the floral transition, a developmental switch that is finely modulated by a complex network of floral pathways that respond to various endogenous and environmental signals (
Andres and Coupland, 2012
;
Bao et al., 2020
;
Liu et al., 2021
). As major downstream integrators regulated by multiple floral pathways, FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) in the model plant
Arabidopsis thaliana
and its orthologs in many other plant species are also essential constituents of the florigen that is transported from leaves to shoot apices to induce flowering (
Tsuji, 2017
;
Liu et al., 2021
). Loss of function of
FT
leads to late flowering under long days, whereas overexpression of
FT
results in extremely early flowering regardless of day length (
Kardailsky et al., 1999
;
Kobayashi et al., 1999
).
FT
expression is specifically activated in the phloem companion cells of the leaf vasculature, and its protein is transported long-distance from leaves to shoot apices, where it interacts with FD and 14-3-3 proteins to activate floral meristem identity genes to initiate flowering (
Takada and Goto, 2003
;
Abe et al., 2005
;
Wigge et al., 2005
;
Corbesier et al., 2007
;
Jaeger and Wigge, 2007
;
Taoka et al., 2011
;
Liu et al., 2012
;
Zhu et al., 2016
).
Specific transcription of
FT
in the leaf vasculature is precisely balanced by a multitude of activators and repressors (
Liu et al., 2021
). Under long days only, the GIGANTEA (GI)–CONSTANS (CO)–
FT
regulatory cascade transmits signals from the photoperiod pathway to transcriptionally activate expression of
FT
in the leaf vasculature in a circadian rhythmic manner (
Putterill et al., 1995
;
Fowler et al., 1999
;
Samach et al., 2000
;
An et al., 2004
;
Wigge et al., 2005
). A repressor complex formed by two MADS-box transcription factors, SHORT VEGETATIVE PHASE (SVP) and FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC), represses
FT
expression by directly binding to the regulatory sequences of
FT
(
Helliwell et al., 2006
;
Lee et al., 2007
;
Li et al., 2008
). SVP also regulates
FT
expression by interacting with different splicing forms of FLOWERING LOCUS M in a temperature-dependent manner to mediate the flowering response to ambient temperature (
Balasubramanian et al., 2006
;
Lee et al., 2007
,
2013
). Interestingly, a direct downstream target of SVP, EARLY FLOWERING MYB PROTEIN (EFM), which encodes a MYB transcription factor, has been shown to directly suppress
FT
expression in the leaf vasculature to mediate the response to ambient temperature and light (
Yan et al., 2014
). Loss of function of
EFM
causes a significant early-flowering phenotype under both long days and short days, which is attributed to increased
FT
expression in the leaf vascular tissues.
Site-specific phosphorylation and dephosphorylation are the most common modifications that influence protein activities or stabilities in various signaling pathways and developmental processes. We previously showed that C-TERMINAL DOMAIN PHOSPHATASE-LIKE 3 (CPL3) activates
FLC
expression by mediating the dephosphorylation of FLX-LIKE 4 (
Shen et al., 2022
) and that CPL2 acts redundantly with CPL3 in
FLC
activation and floral repression (
Zhang and Shen, 2022
). However,
cpl2
flowers much earlier than
flc
(
Shen et al., 2022
;
Zhang and Shen, 2022
), pointing to the presence of other target(s) downstream of CPL2 in flowering. In addition to flowering-time defects,
cpl2
also exhibits smaller leaves, low fertility, and hypersensitivity to salt stress (
Ueda et al., 2008
). Moreover, CPL2 has been shown to mediate the dephosphorylation of RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain-Ser 5 to assist the Bromo adjacent homology–plant homeodomain module in H3K27me3 recognition and transcriptional repression (
Koiwa et al., 2004
;
Zhang et al., 2020
). However, it remains unclear whether CPL2 mediates the dephosphorylation of any specific flowering time regulator(s) to modulate flowering.
In this study, we show that CPL2 directly interacts with and dephosphorylates EFM to facilitate binding of dephosphorylated EFM to
FT
chromatin, thereby suppressing
FT
expression to ensure timely flowering. By contrast, phosphorylated EFM accumulates when CPL2 is absent, resulting in elevated
FT
expression and precocious flowering. Our study suggests that CPL2-mediated dephosphorylation of EFM acts as a molecular switch to repress
FT
expression and thus prevent premature flowering.
Results
CPL2 represses
FT
expression
cpl2-2
mutants exhibited a significant early-flowering phenotype under both long days and short days (
Figures 1
A and 1B;
Supplemental Figure 1A–1D
), as reported previously (
Ueda et al., 2008
;
Zhang et al., 2020
;
Zhang and Shen, 2022
). This early-flowering phenotype of
cpl2-2
was successfully rescued by transformation with a genomic fragment (
gCPL2-3FLAG
or
gCPL2-GFP
) or overexpression construct of
CPL2
(
35S
:
CPL2-3FLAG
or
35S
:
CPL2-GFP
) (
Figures 1
A and 1B;
Supplemental Figure 1
E and 1F), confirming that CPL2 plays an important role in floral repression.

We have previously shown that CPL2 acts redundantly with CPL3 in
FLC
activation and floral repression (
Zhang and Shen, 2022
). However,
cpl2-2
flowered much earlier than
flc-3
under long days (
Shen et al., 2022
;
Zhang and Shen, 2022
) and showed a response to vernalization (
Supplemental Figure 2A
), implying the presence of other target(s) downstream of CPL2 in flowering. To further study the molecular mechanism by which CPL2 represses the floral transition, we performed high-throughput sequencing analysis of RNA isolated from 9-day-old seedlings of the wild type (WT) and
cpl2-2
grown under long days. We identified 601 upregulated and 84 downregulated genes in
cpl2-2
mutants compared with the WT (
ǀ
log
2
(fold change)
ǀ
≥ 1 and adjusted p [padj] ≤ 0.05) (
Figure 1
C;
Supplemental Table 1
). In addition to downregulation of
FLC
, we also observed upregulation of the key floral pathway integrator gene
FT
in
cpl2-2
(
Figure 1
C;
Supplemental Table 1
).
We further examined the temporal expression of
FT
in developing seedlings of WT and
cpl2-2
.
FT
expression was consistently and markedly higher in developing
cpl2-2
seedlings compared with WT plants during the floral transition (
Figure 1
D). Expression of another floral pathway integrator,
SUPPRESSOR OF OVEREXPRESSION OF CONSTANS 1
, was also upregulated in developing
cpl2-2
mutants (
Supplemental Figure 2B
). By contrast, expression of the
FT
activator
CO
was not greatly affected in
cpl2-2
mutants (
Supplemental Figure 2
C and 2E), and
GI
expression was slightly reduced in 7- and 9-day-old seedlings of
cpl2-2
(
Supplemental Figure 2
D and 2F). Because
FT
expression exhibits a diurnal pattern under long days (
Imaizumi and Kay, 2006
), we examined its circadian expression in
cpl2-2
and found that
FT
expression was constantly upregulated in
cpl2-2
mutants over a 24-h period (
Figure 1
E). This result is consistent with the observation that
CPL2
did not show a diurnal expression pattern under long days (
Supplemental Figure 2G
).
FT
expression was also upregulated in
cpl2-2
mutants grown under short days (
Supplemental Figure 2H
), which is in line with its early-flowering phenotype under short days (
Supplemental Figure 1
C and 1D). Moreover,
FT
expression was restored in
cpl2-2 gCPL2-3FLAG
and
cpl2-2 gCPL2-GFP
, whose flowering times were comparable to those of WT plants under long days (
Figures 1
B and 1F). These observations suggest a strong repressive effect of CPL2 on
FT
expression.
We next studied the genetic interaction between
CPL2
and
FT
by generating the
ft-10 cpl2-2
double mutant.
ft-10
almost completely suppressed the early-flowering phenotype of
cpl2-2
(
Figure 1
G), suggesting that
FT
is a major downstream target of CPL2 in flowering time control.
CPL2 mediates
FT
expression in the leaf vasculature
In line with its role in mediating the floral transition, CPL2 was detected in the leaf vasculature, mesophyll cells, and shoot apices of young seedlings before and during the floral transition, as revealed by a
gCPL2-GUS
reporter line in which the same
CPL2
genomic fragment in
gCPL2-3FLAG/GFP
was fused with the
GUS
gene (
Figure 2
A;
Supplemental Figure 3
A). Interestingly, CPL2-GUS signals decreased in older leaves (
Figure 2
A). GUS signals were also found in cauline leaves, floral buds, siliques, and roots (
Supplemental Figure 3
A). We further examined the subcellular localization of CPL2-GFP in
Nicotiana benthamiana
cells and transgenic lines of
cpl2-2 35S
:
CPL2-GFP
and
cpl2-2 gCPL2-GFP
, both expressing functional CPL2-GFP proteins, and found that CPL2-GFP localized in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (
Figure 2
B;
Supplemental Figure 3
B and 3C).

Because
FT
is highly expressed in the leaf vasculature (
Takada and Goto, 2003
), we next examined the spatial effect of CPL2 on
FT
repression. We crossed the
FT
:
GUS
reporter line (
Takada and Goto, 2003
) with
cpl2-2
and found that FT:GUS signals were greatly enhanced in the leaf vasculature of
cpl2-2
compared with WT (
Figure 2
C and 2D). This result indicates that CPL2 represses
FT
expression in the leaf vasculature to inhibit flowering. To further verify this hypothesis, we transformed
cpl2-2
mutants with a
pSUC2
:
CPL2
construct in which expression of the
CPL2
coding sequence was controlled by the promoter of
SUCROSE TRANSPORTER 2
(
SUC2
), which is specifically active in phloem companion cells (
Nelson et al., 2007
). Flowering times of all T1
cpl2-2 pSUC2
:
CPL2
transformants were similar to those of WT plants (
Figure 2
E), supporting the idea that CPL2 functions in the vascular tissues. Together, these data suggest that CPL2 mediates flowering time and
FT
expression in the leaf vasculature.
CPL2 interacts with EFM
Given that CPLs are C-terminal domain phosphatase-like proteins that dephosphorylate multiple regulators to ultimately achieve gene regulation (
Manavella et al., 2012
;
Zhang et al., 2020
;
Shen et al., 2022
), we hypothesized that CPL2 might repress
FT
expression by dephosphorylating upstream regulator(s) of
FT.
We thus proceeded to test whether CPL2 interacted with any known
FT
regulator(s) such as SVP, EFM, FLC, MADS AFFECTING FLOWERING 1, TERMINAL FLOWER 2, CURLY LEAF, EMBRYONIC FLOWER 2, CO, GI, FLAVIN-BINDING KELCH REPEAT F-BOX 1, and phytochrome A (
Takada and Goto, 2003
;
Jiang et al., 2008
;
Liu et al., 2021
). Yeast two-hybrid assays revealed an interaction between CPL2 and EFM (
Figure 3
A;
Supplemental Figure 4
A), a MYB-domain protein that also directly represses
FT
expression in leaf vascular tissues (
Yan et al., 2014
). CPL2 contains an N-terminal catalytic domain and a double-stranded RNA–binding domain at its C terminus (
Figure 3
A) (
Koiwa et al., 2002
). We then examined which domain of CPL2 mediates its interaction with EFM and found that the CPL2-C fragment containing the double-stranded RNA–binding domain interacted with EFM, but the CPL2-N fragment did not (
Figure 3
A). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) analyses further confirmed the interaction between EFM and the C-terminal portion of CPL2 in
N
.
benthamiana
leaf epidermal cells (
Figure 3
B). Moreover, coimmunoprecipitation assays demonstrated the
in vivo
interaction of CPL2-3FLAG and EFM-4HA (hemagglutinin) in the nucleus of
N
.
benthamiana
cells (
Supplemental Figure 4
B) and
Arabidopsis
seedlings expressing functional CPL2-3FLAG and EFM-4HA proteins (
Figure 3
C).

We next analyzed the genetic interaction between
CPL2
and
EFM
. Genetic analyses revealed that
cpl2-2 efm-1
flowered only slightly earlier than
efm-1
(
Figure 3
D and 3E). We further examined
FT
expression in
cpl2-2 efm-1
double mutants and found that
FT
expression was slightly higher in
cpl2-2 efm-1
than in
cpl2-2
and comparable to that in
efm-1
(
Figure 3
F). These observations indicate that CPL2 and EFM are involved in the same flowering pathway dependent on
FT
expression, while also functioning independently in other flowering pathways.
CPL2 dephosphorylates EFM
The
in vivo
interaction between CPL2 and EFM and their overlapping function in flowering time regulation, together with the observation that CPL2 did not affect
EFM
expression (
Supplemental Figure 5
), prompted us to test whether CPL2 dephosphorylates EFM to regulate flowering time. EFM-4HA, when expressed in
Arabidopsis

Discussion
FT
is a potent floral inducer whose transcription is precisely titrated by various floral promoters and repressors to ensure correct timing of flowering and maximum success in plant reproduction (
Liu et al., 2021
). Here, we reveal a hitherto unknown mechanism underlying the timely initiation of flowering, in which the C-terminal domain phosphatase CPL2 directly interacts with and dephosphorylates EFM to facilitate binding of EFM to
FT
chromatin for
FT
repression (
Figure 6
). Loss of function of
CPL2
leads to accumulation of phosphorylated EFM with compromised binding ability to the
FT
locus, resulting in
FT
overproduction and early flowering. Thus, this dephosphorylation-dependent molecular switch is required for suppression of
FT
transcription in leaf vascular tissues to prevent precocious flowering in
Arabidopsis
.

Our findings highlight the significant role played by CPL2 in
FT
repression and flowering time control via modulation of EFM phosphorylation status. The notion that CPL2 and EFM act in the same pathway in
FT
suppression is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence. First, like
efm-1
(
Yan et al., 2014
),
cpl2-2
mutants exhibited significant early-flowering phenotypes with elevated
FT
expression in leaf vascular tissues (
Figures 2
and
3
).
ft-10
almost fully suppressed the early-flowering phenotype of
cpl2-2
or
efm-1
, confirming that
FT
is a major target of CPL2 in flowering time regulation.
cpl2-2 efm-1
flowered sightly earlier than the
efm-1
single mutant (
Figure 3
D), implying that they act both interdependently and in parallel. This is not surprising, because CPL2 has been shown to influence
FLC
expression in mediating flowering time (
Zhang and Shen, 2022
), and our RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data revealed that several other genes relevant to flowering, such as
MAF5
,
LEAFY
(
LFY
), and
AP1
, were differentially expressed in
cpl2
mutants (
Supplemental Table 1
). Second, both CPL2 and EFM function in the leaf vascular tissues to control flowering. Expression of CPL2 and EFM under the leaf vasculature–specific
SUC2
promoter fully rescued their respective mutants (
Figure 2
E;
Yan et al., 2014
), indicating that CPL2 and EFM exert their flowering regulator roles mainly in the leaf vascular tissues, where
FT
is transcribed (
Takada and Goto, 2003
). Third, CPL2 physically interacts with and dephosphorylates EFM. When CPL2 was present, the level of phosphorylated EFM was reduced (
Figure 4
C); by contrast, loss of
CPL2
increased the levels of phosphorylated EFM protein (
Figure 4
F). Together, our data suggest that the CPL2–EFM module suppresses
FT
expression to prevent early flowering.
Dephosphorylation of EFM by CPL2 is involved in regulation of
FT
expression levels and appropriate flowering time. Phosphorylation of EFM at the two consecutive serine residues S147 and S148 failed to rescue the flowering defects of
efm-1
mutants; by contrast, dephosphorylated EFM in which these two serine residues were mutated to alanine fully complemented
efm-1
(
Figure 5
C). Previous work has shown that protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation can profoundly influence the DNA-binding activity of transcription factors (
Horbach et al., 2015
;
Kim et al., 2017
;
Wijeratne et al., 2022
). Likewise, we found that phosphorylation of EFM at two consecutive serine residues abolished its association with the
FT
promoter (
Figure 5
E;
Supplemental Figure 8C
), leading to a failure in suppression of
FT
expression. These results demonstrate that dephosphorylation of EFM by CPL2 is critical for
FT
repression and proper flowering time. Interestingly, despite its function in flowering, dephosphorylated EFM is less abundant than phosphorylated forms
in vivo
, as observed in functional EFM tagging lines (
Figure 4
B), implying that EFM phosphorylation by one or more kinases may be important for antagonizing dephosphorylated EFM–mediated
FT
repression to ensure timely flowering. Thus, a balance between the dephosphorylated and phosphorylated EFM proteins may be important for flowering. It would be intriguing to study how CPL2 and the unknown EFM-phosphorylating kinase(s) act in concert in response to various flowering signals to balance relative levels of dephosphorylated and phosphorylated EFM and fine-tune
FT
expression to eventually modulate flowering.
In conclusion, we have uncovered a CPL2–EFM–
FT
regulatory module in which CPL2 dephosphorylates EFM to facilitate the binding of EFM to the
FT
locus to repress
FT
expression, thereby preventing early flowering. Given the conserved nature of its components across different plant species (
Koiwa et al., 2004
;
Yan et al., 2014
;
Liu et al., 2021
), it would be intriguing to explore whether the CPL2–EFM–
FT
module exists and could be modulated in crop species to fine-tune florigen transcript levels and ensure timely flowering under favorable conditions for subsequent reproductive success.
Methods
Plant materials and growth conditions
Arabidopsis
and
N
.
benthamiana
plants were grown on soil under long days (16-h light/8-h dark) or short days (8-h light/16-h light) at 23°C ± 2°C. Seeds of
cpl2-2
(SALK_059753) were obtained from the
Arabidopsis
Information Resource.
Agrobacterium
-mediated transformation of
Arabidopsis
WT,
cpl2-2
, and
efm-1
mutants was performed using the floral-dip method (
Clough and Bent, 1998
). All transgenic plants generated in the WT,
cpl2-2
, or
efm-1
backgrounds were selected on soil using Basta. In brief, T0 seeds from the transformed plants were directly sown on soil and grown under long days. Basta (0.2% v/v, Basta, Bayer) was sprayed evenly onto the seedlings at 3 and 10 days after germination. The surviving T1 seedlings were transferred to new soil, and the number of rosette leaves was counted when the plants had bolted to 10 cm. T3 transgenic plants were sown on soil, and the number of rosette leaves was counted in a similar manner.
Plasmid construction
A series of modified pENTR vectors were generated for construction of the plasmids used in this study. A sequence containing multiple cloning sites and a terminator was amplified from pGreen-0229 (
Hellens et al., 2000
) and cloned into pENTR/D-TOPO (Invitrogen) to generate the modified pENTR vector (
Shen et al., 2016
). The coding sequence of
GUS
was cloned into this modified vector to generate pENTR-GUS. Similarly, a sequence containing a 2×
35S
promoter, multiple cloning sites, and a terminator was amplified from pGreen-35S-0229 (
Yu et al., 2004
) to generate the pENTR-35S vector. The coding sequences of
4HA
,
FLAG
, and
GFP
were cloned into pENTR-35S to generate pENTR-35S-4HA, pENTR-35S-FLAG, and pENTR-35S-GFP, respectively.
To construct
gCPL2-3FLAG
and
gCPL2-GFP
, the 6.8-kb genomic sequence of
CPL2
containing the 2.0-kb upstream sequence, the 4.0-kb coding sequence plus introns, and the 0.8-kb downstream sequence was amplified with gCPL2-F (
EcoR
V) and gCPL2-R (
Xma
I) and cloned into the modified pENTR vector to generate
gCPL2
. The
Kpn
I restriction site was cloned before the stop codon by a modified QuickChange site-directed mutagenesis method (
Geiser et al., 2001
) to generate
gCPL2
(
Kpn
I). Using this construct,
gCPL2-3FLAG
and
gCPL2-GFP
were generated by cloning the corresponding sequences of 3FLAG and GFP into the
Kpn
I site. To construct
gCPL2-GUS
, the genomic sequence of
CPL2
was amplified with primers gCPL2-F (
EcoR
V) and gCPL2-GUS-R (
Xma
I) and cloned into pENTR-GUS. To construct
35S
:
CPL2-3FLAG
and
35S
:
CPL2-GFP
, the coding sequence of
CPL2
was amplified with CPL2-F (
EcoR
I) and CPL2-R (
Xma
I) and cloned into the pENTR-35S-3FLAG and pENTR-35S-GFP vectors, respectively. The resulting entry constructs were introduced into the binary vector pBGW through the Gateway LR recombination reaction (Invitrogen).
To construct
35S
:
EFM-4HA
, the coding sequence of
EFM
was amplified with EFM-F (
Pst
I) and EFM-R (
Xma
I) and cloned into pENTR-35S-4HA. Using this construct,

:
EFM-4HA
S147A S148A
and
35S
:
EFM-4HA
S147D S148D

). The resulting entry constructs were introduced into the binary vector pBGW through the Gateway LR recombination reaction (Invitrogen). The primers used for plasmid construction are listed in
Supplemental Table 2
.
RNA-seq
The aerial parts of 9-day-old WT and
cpl2-2
seedlings grown under long days were harvested at ZT12. Total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, then quantified and examined on an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system. mRNA was purified from total RNA using poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads. Libraries were constructed with the NEB-Next Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB), and sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform.
Expression analysis
Total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. After extraction, RNA was reverse transcribed using M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase (Promega). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed with SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a QuantStudio 5 Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems). Expression of
TUB2
was included as an internal control. Gene expression levels were determined as described previously (
Li et al., 2008
). The real-time primers used to analyze gene expression are shown in
Supplemental Table 2
. The GUS staining and activity assays for
gCPL2-GUS
,
FT
:
GUS
, and
cpl2-2 FT
:

;

). Photographs were taken under a light microscope.

cpl2-2 gCPL2-3FLAG
and

:

or

.

leaves co-infiltrated with

After extensive washing steps, the immunoprecipitated proteins and nuclear extracts (as input) were analyzed by immunoblotting with anti-HA (Santa Cruz) and anti-FLAG (Sigma-Aldrich) antibodies.
CIAP treatment
CIAP treatment of EFM protein was performed as described previously (
Wang et al., 2010
). In brief, EFM-4HA proteins from
efm-1 35S
:
EFM-4HA
transgenic plants or protoplasts transfected with
35S
:
EFM-4HA
were immunoprecipitated with anti-HA agarose (Sigma-Aldrich). After two washes with alkaline buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl [pH 8.8], 1 mM MgCl
2
) and one wash with CIAP buffer, the agarose beads were incubated with or without CIAP for 3 h at 37°C. The proteins were then analyzed by SDS–PAGE with or without Phos-tag followed by immunoblot analysis with anti-HA antibody (Santa Cruz).
Phos-tag SDS–PAGE
Phos-tag SDS–PAGE was carried out as described previously (
Chen et al., 2020
). Phos-tag (50 μM; Wako Pure Chemical Industries) and MnCl
2
(100 μM) were added to the separation gels of SDS–PAGE. After electrophoresis, the Phos-tag gels were washed three times with transfer buffer (25 mM Tris, 192 mM glycine, 20% methanol) supplemented with 10 mM EDTA, washed once with transfer buffer, blotted, and detected with anti-HA antibody (Santa Cruz).
Mass spectrometry analysis
Nuclear proteins were extracted from 9-day-old seedlings of
efm-1 35S
:
EFM-4HA
using the nuclear isolation buffer described above, freshly supplemented with 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) and 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 3 (Sigma-Aldrich), and resuspended in immunoprecipitation buffer supplemented with 1× protease inhibitor cocktail and 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail. After immunoprecipitation with anti-HA agarose (Sigma-Aldrich), the immunoprecipitated proteins were eluted by heating and analyzed by mass spectrometry with a TripleTOF 5600 System (AB Sciex, Protein and Proteomics Center, National University of Singapore).
EMSA
The full-length sequences of
EFM
,
EFM
S147A S148A
, and
EFM
S147D S148D
were cloned into the pGEX-6p-2 vector (Pharmacia). The resulting vectors were transformed into
Escherichia coli
Rosetta (DE3) cells (Novagen). Production of the recombinant proteins was induced by isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside at 16°C overnight, and the proteins were affinity purified using Glutathione Sepharose beads (Amersham Bioscience) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. EMSA was performed using the LightShift Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (Thermo Fisher).
ChIP assay
The ChIP assay was performed using various plants as described previously (
Shen et al., 2011
). In brief, 9-day-old seedlings were collected, ground in liquid nitrogen, and fixed in 1% formaldehyde for 10 min. The fixation reaction was stopped by addition of glycine. Subsequently, chromatin was extracted, sonicated to produce DNA fragments approximately 500 bp in size, and incubated with anti-HA agarose conjugate (Sigma) for 4 h at 4°C. After extensive washing, the protein–DNA complexes were eluted from the beads, reverse crosslinked, and treated with proteinase K (Roche). DNA was recovered using the QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen). ChIP enrichment was determined by quantitative real-time PCR on a QuantStudio Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems). The primer pairs used for ChIP assays are shown in
Supplemental Table 2
.
Statistical analysis
Details of the statistical analyses are provided in the figure legends. Immunoblot signals were quantified using ImageJ (
https://imagej.net/ij/index.html
